Text: {{c1::Certification::process}} is the exam-based verification that a provider meets {{c2::minimum competency standards}} for emergency care.
Back Extra: Distinguish: Certification verifies competency; licensure is the legal authority to practice; credentialing is an employer's check of qualifications.

Text: {{c1::Licensure::status}} is the {{c2::legal authority to practice}} in your state, granted after you complete certification.
Back Extra: Distinguish: Certification verifies you meet competency standards; licensure is the state granting legal authority to practice.

Text: {{c1::Credentialing::process}} is the verification of a health care provider's {{c2::qualifications}}, the phase after licensure, often overseen by a medical director.
Back Extra: Cue: Credentialing can grant an EMT additional skills or limit them, beyond the base scope of practice.

Text: The four EMS licensure levels, from least to most training, are {{c1::emergency medical responder (EMR)}}, {{c1::EMT}}, {{c1::advanced EMT (AEMT)}}, and {{c1::paramedic}}.
Back Extra: Cue: Each level has a wider scope of practice; EMR is the most basic, paramedic the most advanced.

Text: Beyond the EMT level, an AEMT adds selected {{c1::advanced life support (ALS)::level of care}} skills such as IV and IO therapy, advanced airway adjuncts, and a limited number of medications.
Back Extra: Distinguish: An AEMT has more than an EMT but less than a paramedic, who carries the full ALS scope.

Text: The AEMT course typically ranges from {{c1::200 to 400::hours}} hours.
Back Extra: Cue: More than an EMT course (about 150 to 200 hours) and well short of full paramedic training.

Text: The core work of an EMT on a call follows four steps: {{c1::scene size-up}}, {{c1::patient assessment}}, {{c1::treatment}}, and {{c1::transport}}.
Back Extra: Cue: Size up the scene (is it safe?), assess to find life threats, treat, then transport the patient to definitive care.

Text: The six EMS functions on the bars of the Star of Life, in order, are {{c1::detection}}, {{c1::reporting}}, {{c1::response}}, {{c1::on-scene care}}, {{c1::care in transit}}, and {{c1::transfer to definitive care}}.
Back Extra: Cue: They trace a call from spotting the emergency (detection) to hospital handoff (transfer to definitive care).

Text: {{c1::Title I::which title?}} of the Americans with Disabilities Act protects EMTs with disabilities seeking employment, requiring covered employers to make reasonable accommodations.
Back Extra: Cue: Accommodations let an EMT who can perform the job's functional skills pursue the career despite a disability.

Text: Because licensure is a {{c1::state::level of government}} function, the laws regulating how EMS providers operate are enacted at the state level.
Back Extra: Cue: The state EMS office controls licensure; the local medical director provides day-to-day oversight.

Text: A medical director can {{c1::limit::limit or expand?}} an EMT's scope of practice but cannot expand it beyond what state law already allows.
Back Extra: Pitfall: Adding a skill the state has not approved requires state approval first, not just the medical director's permission.

Text: The EMS Agenda 2050 envisions an EMS system that is {{c1::inherently safe and effective}}, {{c1::integrated and seamless}}, {{c1::reliable and prepared}}, {{c1::socially equitable}}, {{c1::sustainable and efficient}}, and {{c1::adaptable and innovative}}.
Back Extra: Cue: Six guiding principles, anchor each by one word: safety, integration, reliability, equity, sustainability, adaptability.

Text: A {{c1::medical director::role}} is the physician who {{c2::authorizes a service's EMTs to provide care}} and to whom treatment problems or procedure changes are referred.
Back Extra: Cue: The medical director is the working liaison between the EMTs, the hospitals, and the medical community.

Text: {{c1::Standing orders::term}} let an EMT act on a specific complaint or condition {{c2::without contacting medical control first}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: Standing orders are pre-authorized, off-line care; they are part of the written protocols.

Text: The medical director approves the required {{c1::continuing education and training}} for each EMT in the service.
Back Extra: Cue: This keeps every EMT's knowledge and skills current and meeting the proper training standards.

Text: The two forms of medical control are off-line, also called {{c1::indirect}}, and online, also called {{c1::direct}}.
Back Extra: Cue: Off-line / indirect = orders set up in advance; online / direct = live direction during the call.

Text: {{c1::Online::which?}} (direct) medical control is {{c2::real-time direction by phone or radio during a call}}, from the medical director or a designated physician.
Back Extra: Distinguish: Off-line control is set up ahead of time (standing orders, protocols); online happens live during the call.

Text: {{c1::Off-line::which?}} (indirect) medical control is {{c2::standing orders, protocols, training, and supervision set up in advance}} by the medical director.
Back Extra: Distinguish: Online control is live phone or radio direction during a call; off-line is established beforehand.

Text: {{c1::Mobile integrated health care (MIH)::model}} delivers health care using {{c2::prehospital resources, within the community}}, rather than at a physician's office or hospital.
Back Extra: Cue: MIH aims to improve access to care at an affordable price and connects patients with resources like social services.

Text: The medical director is responsible for {{c1::quality control::responsibility}}, ensuring everyone under their supervision meets appropriate medical-care standards on each call.
Back Extra: Cue: Quality oversight runs from the medical director down to each individual EMT's own practice.

Text: {{c1::Continuous quality improvement (CQI)::process}} is a quality-management process in which team members at every level keep asking {{c2::'how are we doing now, and how can we do better?'}}
Back Extra: Cue: CQI is proactive and ongoing, not a one-time inspection; it depends on a just culture that reports errors without blame.

Text: Medical errors are commonly grouped into three sources: a {{c1::rules-based}}, a {{c1::knowledge-based}}, or a {{c1::skills-based}} failure.
Back Extra: Cue: Rules = did the wrong thing per protocol or permission; knowledge = did not know; skills = could not perform it correctly.

Text: {{c1::Public health::field}} examines the health needs of {{c2::entire populations}}, with the goal of preventing health problems.
Back Extra: Distinguish: Public health is proactive and population-level; emergency care is reactive and patient-level.

Text: A {{c1::goiter::condition}} is an abnormally large thyroid gland, caused by too little {{c2::iodine}} in the diet.
Back Extra: Ex: Adding iodine to table salt is a classic public-health measure that made goiters rare in the US.

Text: {{c1::Primary::primary or secondary?}} prevention is {{c2::stopping an event from ever happening}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: Secondary prevention acts after the event to reduce its effects. Ex: a vaccine is primary prevention.

Text: {{c1::Secondary::primary or secondary?}} prevention is {{c2::reducing the effects of an event that has already happened}}.
Back Extra: Distinguish: Primary prevention stops the event entirely. Ex: seatbelts and helmets are secondary, reducing injury in a crash.

Text: A {{c1::patient advocate::role}} is an EMT who does everything with {{c2::the patient's best interest in mind}}.
Back Extra: Cue: 'Everything you do needs to be done with the patient in mind' is the guiding principle of EMS.
